doctrine: The Two Natures of Christ, The Hypostatic Union
summary: Christ is fully God and fully man, two natures united in one person without confusion or division (Chalcedon)
readingInstruction: Read Philippians 2:5-11 and Hebrews 2:14-18. Today is a doctrinal pause on Christ as fully God and fully man. Read the Christ hymn slowly, perhaps several times. Notice what Christ was, what he did, and what God did in response.
settingTheScene: Philippians 2:5-11 is often called the Christ hymn, and many scholars think it is an early Christian hymn or creed that Paul quotes. Hebrews 2 makes a similar point about Christ’s humanity. The church fought for centuries to express this truth precisely. At the Council of Chalcedon in AD 451, it confessed that Christ is one person in two natures, truly God and truly man, without confusion, change, division, or separation.
observation: “Though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped” (Philippians 2:6).
“But emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men” (Philippians 2:7).
“And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:8).
“Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:9).
“And every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:11).
“He himself likewise partook of the same things” (Hebrews 2:14).
“Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect” (Hebrews 2:17).
“For because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted” (Hebrews 2:18).
doctrinalFocus:
The church confesses that Jesus Christ is fully God and fully man in one person. This is sometimes called the hypostatic union, or the doctrine of the two natures. It is the climax of the New Testament’s teaching about who Jesus is, and every other doctrine about him depends on it.

Fully God: The New Testament calls Jesus God (John 1:1; 20:28; Titus 2:13), gives him divine names, attributes, and works, and calls for worship of him. In Philippians 2:6, he existed “in the form of God” and had “equality with God.” Fully man: He was born of a woman, grew, hungered, thirsted, wept, was tempted, suffered, and died. He had a human body and a human soul. Hebrews insists he was made like us in every respect, except without sin (4:15). He is one person, not two. The same “I” who is God is the “I” who hungers.

Why does this matter? Because only a man could die for sinners, and only God could bear the infinite weight of sin and conquer death. A mediator between God and man must be both (1 Timothy 2:5). He represents us as one of us and reveals the Father as God. If Jesus is not fully God, he cannot save; if he is not fully man, he cannot save us as one of us. As Gregory of Nazianzus said, “What has not been assumed has not been healed.”

The phrase “emptied himself” (kenosis) has been debated. Orthodox interpretation holds that Christ did not cease to be God or lay aside any divine attribute, but emptied himself by taking on the form of a servant, veiling his glory, and voluntarily limiting the use of his divine prerogatives. He remained fully God while living as a real man. The main sense is not subtraction but addition: he added humanity to his deity. Some modern views claim that he gave up divine attributes; the church has rejected that as inconsistent with the biblical testimony.

The pattern of the hymn is humiliation and exaltation. He descended: from the form of God to the form of a servant, to death, to death on a cross. Then God exalted him with the name above every name, “Lord,” the name of God in the Greek Old Testament. Every knee will bow. This quotes Isaiah 45:23, where it is spoken of Yahweh. Paul applies it to Jesus.
interpretation:
Paul introduces the hymn to teach humility: “Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus.” The model of selfless love is Christ himself. “Though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped.” Christ did not hold onto the privileges of deity as something to exploit. “But emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men.” The Eternal Son took a human nature. “And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.” Crucifixion was the most shameful death. The Son of God went all the way down.

“Therefore God has highly exalted him.” The cross was not the end. The one who humbled himself is exalted. “The name that is above every name” is likely “Lord” (verse 11). “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” Notice that the exaltation of Jesus brings glory to the Father, not rivalry. The whole creation, willingly or not, will acknowledge him.

Hebrews 2 covers the same ground from a different angle. “Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery.” Christ became human in order to die, and he died in order to defeat death and free us from its fear. “Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in the service of God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people. For because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted.” Jesus knows our weakness from the inside. We have a sympathetic high priest.

This is the gospel in its fullest form. God did not remain at a distance. He came near, became one of us, and gave himself for us. And now the one who suffered is reigning.
connection: John 1:1-18 and Colossians 1:15-20 speak of the eternal Word becoming flesh. Isaiah 45:22-25 is the source of Philippians 2:10-11. Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12 foretells the servant’s humiliation and exaltation. Hebrews 4:14-16 speaks of the sympathetic high priest. 1 Timothy 2:5 speaks of one mediator. Romans 1:3-4 mentions both natures. 2 Corinthians 8:9 speaks of his becoming poor. Luke 2:52 says Jesus increased in wisdom and stature. Mark 13:32 shows the limits of his human knowledge. Acts 2:32-36 speaks of God making him Lord and Christ.
application:
Read the Christ hymn aloud each morning this week. Let it shape your attitude toward others.

When you are tempted or suffering, remember that Jesus knows what it is like. Go to him.

Bow the knee. Confess aloud, “Jesus Christ is Lord.”
prayerPrompts: Worship Jesus, who was in the form of God and became a servant.
Thank him for becoming fully human to save you.
Ask him to give you his mindset.
